They may also infect their offspring to cause ophthalmia neonatorum (see Neo- natal Conjunctivitis, p.180) or pneumonia (p.186). Infect- ed pregnant women should be treated and the following regimens have been recommended: • WHO: treatment for 7 days with: • oral erythromycin 500 mg four times daily or • oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily • UK: • as for WHO, or • oral erythromycin 500 mg twice daily for 14 days, or • a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g • USA: • a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g or • oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days alternatives are: • erythromycin-containing regimens Sexual partners of those infected with C. trachomatis should be tested and treated.2-4 For further reference to sexually transmitted C. trachoma- tis infections, see under Epididymitis (p.170), Pelvic In- flammatory Disease (p.184), and Urethritis (p.199) Specific serotypes of C. trachomatis are responsible for another sexually transmitted disease, lymphogranuloma venereum (p.192). Reactive arthritis (see Bone and Joint Infections, p.164) may be secondary to chlamydial infections. Other C. trachomatis infections that are not sexually trans- mitted include trachoma and inclusion conjunctivitis in adults (see Trachoma, p.196). 1. US Preventive Services Task Force.
